2000 CanLII 21409 (CA IRB)
T98-10291 
 The facts giving rise to this application for reinstatement are as follows. The applicant, XXXXXXXXXXXX, was referred to th e Convention Refugee Determination Division (CRDD) on December 30, 1998. On May 11, 1999, the Minister filed a Notice of Intent to Participate in his refugee hearing. In the notice, the Minister contended that matters involving Articles 1(F)(a) and 1(F)(b) were at issue. In July, the Refugee Board sent a Notice of Hearing for September 1, 1999. On August 24, 1999, the applicant signed a written notice withdrawing his claim to Convention refugee status. On August 31, 1999, the applicant married a Canadian citizen, XXXXXXXXXXX, whom he had met in April. On September 3, 1999, the applicant's spouse filed an application to sponsor her husband. The applicant and his wife separated, and have lived separate and apart since XXXXXXXX X, 1999. On November 12, 1999, Ms. XXXXXX wrot e to Canada Immigration officials withdrawing her sponsorship application. On December 13, 1999, the applicant filed a Humanitarian and Compassionate application with Canada Immigration. On XXXXXXX XX, 2000, the applicant was arrested and charged with a number of offenses. On January 28, 2000, the applicant filed this motion to reinstate his refugee claim. Under the CRDD Rules, a refugee claimant can, at any time, withdraw his claim to Convention refugee status. Subsequently, he may apply to have the claim reinstated and the Refugee Division may reinstate the claim "if it is satisfied that there are sufficient reasons why the claim . . . should be reinstated and that it is in the interests of justice to do so."
1 The test is, therefore, twofold. There mu st be sufficient reasons to reinstate and it must be in the interests of justice to do so. There is little guidance as to how one should interpret this test although I have reviewed three recent decisions by colleagues in Ottawa and Vancouver.
2 I have considered the following factors under the rubric of "sufficient reasons" – whether the withdrawal was inform ed and whether the withdrawal was for a valid reason. 
 
1 Rule 34. 
2 CRDD A93-80785, Noseworthy, March 30, 19 95; CRDD V07-03611, Jackson, September 22, 1999; CRDD V98-00402, Jackson, June 7, 1999. 
2000 CanLII 21409 (CA IRB)
T98-10291 
 2 Was the withdrawal informed?
 People who do not understand what they are doing when they withdraw their claims should not be prejudiced.
3 The applicant in this case had counsel at the time of his withdrawal. In fact, a review of his file reveals that he has retained four counsel over the course of the last 18 months, all well known members of the immigration bar in Toronto. The applicant states that he withdrew his clai m on the advice of his then counsel because he was being sponsored by a woman he was about to marry who was a Canadian citizen. In the absence to any evidence to the contrary, I assume that the applicant was advised of the implications of his withdrawal and I find that the withdrawal was informed. Was the withdrawal of the refugee claim for a good reason?
 The applicant was getting married to a Ca nadian citizen and was so married a few days after he notified the Refugee Division of his withdrawal. There is some evidence to suggest that the marriage was for purposes of immigration. The timing of the marriage gives rise to this concern as does the letter of XXXXXXXXXXX withdrawing her sponsorship. However, the task of determining if a marriage is genuine or entered into for immigration purposes is a credibility exercise and I cannot conclude, on the basis of the evidence before me, that the marriage was one of convenience. There may be some cases, where withdrawing the refugee claim to gain landing through another means is not to be discouraged when one considers the expense and resources of parallel processing. However, it does not seem reasonable to me that if the other process fails that the applicant should be reinstated automatically. As noted by my colleague in CRDD V98-00402
, to do so would amount to a de facto adjournment that is not time limited. This is not in harmony with s.69(6) of the Immigration Act
 which directs the Refugee Division to adjourn only if the adjournment would not unreasonably impede the proceedings of the Board. 
 
3 CRDD A93-080785, XXXXXXXXXX, March 30, 1995. 
2000 CanLII 21409 (CA IRB)
T98-10291 
 3 The applicant before me did not save the Board any expense or economy by withdrawing his refugee claim whe n he di d. XXXXXX s la te filing his Personal Information Form (PIF) which resulted in his claim going into No PIF Abandonment Court and he chose to withdraw one week before his claim was to be heard. By this time the Board had been put to considerable expense preparing for th e hearing and would not have been in the position at that late date to schedule another matter for the assigned panel. I find that the applicant has failed to provide sufficient reasons why his claim to Convention refugee status should be reinstated. It is in the interests of justice to reinstate the applicant’s claim? I have considered three factors under this heading – whether there was undue delay in seeking re-instatement; whether the charges that the applicant faces sh ould have any bearing on this application; and whether there are good reasons to hear the applicant’s refugee claim on the merits. Was there undue delay?
 When the couple separated on XXXXXXXX X, 1999, and the applicant did two things. He filed for humanitarian and compa ssionate consideration and he began to seek advice about reinstating his claim to Convention refugee status. In my view, with respect to reinstatement, it is important that the applicant demonstrate that he acted very quickly to seek reinstatement after the break up of the marriage. This is because once he withdraws his claim, the applicant's conditional removal order becomes effective and delay on his part could suggest a lack of interest with respect to his immigration status. I disagree with counsel for the Minister that had the applicant been interested in pursuing his refugee claim, he would not have gone the humanitarian and compassionate route first. Under the provisions of the Immigration Manual
 where a spousal sponsorship is withdrawn, a humanitarian and compassionate review would appear to be the norm. 
2000 CanLII 21409 (CA IRB)
T98-10291 
 4s. 9.14(3)(b) If the request has not yet been processed, the case will be reviewed to determine if the spouse can become successfully established and if there are compassionate and humani tarian considerations which would warrant the continued processing of the case to landing.
4 This is an avenue offered to all
 applicants caught by a marriage break-down and, in my opinion, it was quite reasonable that the applicant apply for this consideration as it is part and parcel of the spousal policy. The evidence before me is that he was, at the same time, trying to get legal aid in place in order to apply for the reinstatement of his claim to Convention refugee status. All this occurred within one month of his marriage break-down. In the circumstances, this cannot be said to be undue delay. Are the criminal charges relevant?
 In my opinion, the fact that the applicant has been charged with offences under the Criminal Code
 cannot prejudice him with respect to the reinstatement of his refugee claim. Had he been convicted, this might not be the case, but the presumption of innocence is an overarching value in our justice system that weighs in favour the applicant in this case. Are there good reasons to hear the applicant’s refugee claim on the merits?
 In his PIF, the applicant outlines his fear of persecution should he return to Lebanon and in his affidavit in support of this application, he states that he still fears persecution at the hands of Hezbollah should he return to Lebanon. I agree with counsel for the applicant that the applicant has not had his claim determined on the merits. However, he withdrew of his own volition. The act of withdrawing a claim indicates that a person is no longer seeking protection as a Convention refugee. The applicant has not advanced any additional evidence with respect to his refugee claim that explains how his situation has changed since the date of the withdrawal of his claim.
5 
 
4 Immigration Manual 
5 Supra, footnote 2. 
2000 CanLII 21409 (CA IRB)
T98-10291 
 5 I find that although there was no delay of any significance, the applicant has not demonstrated why he is now seeking protec tion when he had the chance to do so in September 1999 and voluntarily gave up that opportunity. Having considered the above, I find that the applicant has not demonstrated sufficient reasons why the claim should be reinstated. Nor is it in the interest of justice to do so. The application to reinstate the claim to Convention refugee status XXXXXX XXXXX is denied. “XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX” 
 XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX DATED at Toronto, this 23
rd day of February, 2000.
